recommended_response.body:
Two things cost you the most in a diminished value claim, and both are avoidable.

First, evidence structure. The itemised repair invoice matters more than the total. Carriers discount cosmetic work and pay more where structural, safety or ADAS/calibration lines appear, so a single total line reads as cosmetic even when the work wasn't. Pull the itemised invoice and point at the parts/labour split.

Second, comparables beat formulas. Most carriers quote roughly 10% of the physical damage cost, adjusted for age and mileage. The NAIC notes that approach grew out of a single Georgia Supreme Court case and has no legal basis in other states, and that it can double-count mileage because mileage is already priced into standard vehicle values. Use that number to sanity-check a lowball - you cannot use it as your evidence, because an adjuster can discount a formula. What they cannot easily discount is a valuation of your exact year, trim and mileage in clean condition versus with the accident reported, ideally backed by a dealer or trade-in letter in dollars.

One practical point that often decides the outcome: be clear about when you plan to sell or trade. An insurer's strongest argument is that the loss is unrealised if you keep the car. Telling them you are trading within a specific timeframe - and backing it with real trade offers - removes most of that argument.

Also worth knowing before you sign anything: a release signed after repairs and after the DV payment can surrender claims you didn't know you had. That signature is routinely the most expensive one in the file.

And ask them, in writing, to show the calculation behind their figure. They often are not required to, but the request frequently moves the offer.
